title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: the Nyaya Sutra sorts every argument into three kinds of talk, and only one of them is looking for the truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nyaya's argument in five parts, said out loud, with the example doing the real work: where's your pot? A new week begins.

Three arguments are going on at the same wedding. At one table, two old friends are working out whether a hard decision was right, and each keeps saying, wait, say that again, I think you've got a point. At the next table, two uncles are arguing politics, and neither one is listening; each is just waiting for a gap to land the next blow. And in the corner, somebody has no opinion of his own at all. He just pokes holes in whatever anyone else says. Same noise. Same raised hands. The Nyaya Sutra says these are three different things, and it gives each one a name.
screen: `THREE ARGUMENTS, ONE WEDDING.` → `SAME NOISE, DIFFERENT AIMS.` → `NYAYA NAMES ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: The first is vada: discussion. In the Nyaya Sutra, vada is talk where both sides use the real means of knowing, perception, inference and the rest, and set out their reasons in yesterday's five parts, without contradicting their own starting points. The point isn't to win. It's to find out. Later the Sutra says vada is the kind of talk you have with a teacher, a student or fellow seekers, people who aren't jealous of being right. The second is jalpa: wrangling. Same parts, but now the aim is victory, so it reaches for tricks: twisting a word into a meaning the speaker never intended, raising objections that only sound like objections. The third is vitanda: cavil. Wrangling with no position of your own. You defend nothing. You only knock down. So far, one good kind of talk and two bad ones. But the Sutra adds a turn. Jalpa and vitanda have a use: they guard a true conclusion the way a hedge of thorny branches guards a sprouting seed. When someone comes only to trample, you may need thorns. So Nyaya doesn't pretend hard argument never happens. It asks you to know which kind you're in, and to remember the hedge exists for the seed. The seed is the truth, and the garden is vada. At a kitchen table, that becomes a practical question, halfway through any argument: am I trying to find out, or trying to win?
screen: `VADA: TALK THAT WANTS TO FIND OUT.` · `JALPA: TALK THAT WANTS TO WIN.` · `VITANDA: ONLY KNOCKING DOWN.` · `THORNS THAT GUARD A SEED.` · then, large: `FIND OUT, OR WIN?`

segments.voice: Replay one recent disagreement, at home, at work or online, without rearguing it; just watch it, as if from the next table. Was it vada, jalpa or vitanda, for you and for the other person? Then find the one honest question your next sentence could have been, and if you pray, ask for a mind that wants the truth more than the win.
Nyaya. Today, its three kinds of talk: vada, discussion that seeks the truth; jalpa, wrangling to win; and vitanda, attacking with no position of your own.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. The thorns are there to guard the seed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit learning, Nyaya students practice vada, structured discussion with a teacher or fellow students, and formal debate, with each side setting out its reasons step by step, has a place in the tradition.

chat.meaning: The Nyaya Sutra names three kinds of talk: vada seeks the truth, jalpa seeks victory with tricks, and vitanda only attacks, with no position of its own.
